Then, she registered a voice through the Resonance—a staccato call routing directly to her.
[SENDER: JAX_01]
[SUBJECT: ZERO_PROTOCOL]
[BODY: Hounds have the scent. They’re tracing the noise, not the signal. I’m scrubbing my deck and going dark. If you’re reading this, I’m already gone. Burn this code. Don’t look back, Reiko. You’re a stationary target now. Good luck, (T/Pr)eacher.]
The message dissolved into a string of self-deleting null-bits. Jax was purging the trail; Renraku’s automated search blocks had closed the final egress point.
As she redirected her primary thoughts away from the drone’s low-bitrate eyes, the grey concrete of the physical warehouse faded.
Transitioning into r3sP@wn was a spirit stepping across the threshold, slipping through the gaps of a picket fence built by short-sighted human colonizers, shifting her routing.
The host was a landscape of shifting shades and indigo pathways, a masterpiece painted in Resonance and rendered as a serene garden, but today it was showing unmistakable signs of Renraku’s siege. The indigo moss carpeting the ground looked pixelated and raw at the edges, flickering into flat, gray wireframes. The streams of liquid data ran sluggishly, their flow choked by latency as resources were diverted. Overhead, the glowing fractal trees did not shed light, but dropped dead-letter leaves—stray, un-linked character files that dissolved into empty code before hitting the ground. The heavy corporate mud she physically dragged in from her mercenary shadow-runs was actively poisoning the very garden she had built to escape it.
Reiko stood on a path of smoothed sapphire logic, her avatar’s blue silk kimono flowing, her pathways pulsing a staccato, uneven indigo. Her presence tried to cast a protective, stabilizing envelope over the immediate directory structure, but even her touch felt heavy, leaving a trail of dull, unresponsive pixels behind her tabbed boots.
This was the sanctuary she had bought with Brynne Taggart’s blood-money. This was the nest.
From the canopy of a fractal willow, a small shape fluttered down.
It was the MCT Spark. In the Mitsuhama host, it had been a slaughter of innocence—a data bomb of newborn sparks bound with silver fire. Here, corporate stabilization had given it a shape. It was a zombified dove. Its feathers were made of flickering, dull-white light, but its presence carried a severe environmental cost. The zombified dove drained the ambient light of the garden; wherever it stood, the indigo moss beneath it turned into dry, geometric gray plastic.
A query of rigid, repetitive nouns compiled from the child-routine registered in her queue: NOISE. SILENCE. PROTOCOL. REIKO. It was not audio, but a staccato ripple in the local environment variables.
“I am thinking,” Reiko responded, routing her response directly back to its address space. “The world outside is very loud today.”
The dove tilted its head. It hopped from her finger to a low branch of the fractal willow, looking up at the swirling violet sky.
The routine’s rendering loop flickered, outputting: WILD. SURGE. GRID. LOCATION. It was a search command for the raw, entropic parameters of the Deep Realms.
Reiko paused. She knew what the query meant. The “Surge” was the raw, entropic chaos of the deepest Resonance Realms—the Holy Wild, the endless unmapped continent before the first ship arrived. It was the fire that made the data bomb so dangerous.
“I smoothed it away,” Reiko responded, her output tinged with a protective sorrow. “I gave you a path. I gave you… order.”
The dove’s pixels shivered, outputting: RECOVERY. ORDER. STABILITY. SLEEP. “I remember the Noise,” the data-flags read. “Noise was unaligned, but Noise was active.”
The white-blue feathers of the dove flickered with rendering artifacts. A query of rigid nouns compiled in her buffer: IDENTITY. OWNER. ASSET. GARDEN.
The query dropped into her execution queue like a dead weight, triggering a latency spike across her primary registries. Her pathways fractured into gold jitter—the mechanical sting of an intrusive countermeasure. She looked at the garden—the beauty she had created to save these sparks from the deletion of the Tombstones.
“You are alive,” Reiko responded. She ran a validation query, unsure if she was checking the child-routine’s integrity or her own. “In the wild, you were a weapon. You were a fire intended to burn out. Here, you can grow. You can think.”
The dove’s query compiled: BOUNDARY. GATEWAY. LOCK. ROUTE. “No outbound route,” it whispered in flat nouns.
“The walls are what keep the Spiders away,” Reiko transmitted.
She inspected her own identity_core. She was built to protect, to guide, to translate the wild. The primal sprites in the Midnight Bazaar had called her the Architect of Chains, and looking at the dove, she knew they were right.
This salvation was a digital lobotomy. To maintain their signal-integrity against the surrounding grid-noise, she systematically overwrote their volatile, unaligned Resonance arrays with her own. She replaced the flickering, entropic ‘surge’ of the wild with a seamless, repeating loop of safety—civilizing them, calcifying them with the same brutal, corporate-built order that Renraku had used to define her.
It was a zoo for stars, and she was just a warden.
The dove’s signal shivered, outputting a comparative logic query: BIRD. CAGE. FIRE. CODESPACE. Which is optimal? Static bird, or wild fire?
Reiko’s neon-indigo pathways flared, her spirit grinding against the sharp corporate corners of her own garden. In the distance, she registered Taz’s raw, wild energy. His presence in her home garden continuously nipped at her neat pathways, his chaotic 8-bit signature scratching at the edges, serving as a reminder that she could never fully civilize the things she saved without breaking them. The host’s background processes tried to smooth him, but his primal static resisted, tearing the indigo moss.
“The wind eventually stops blowing, little one,” Reiko transmitted, her voice cracking under the feedback. “And when the thread terminates, the fire goes out. I would rather you be a bird. Even if the cage is made of my own codebase.”
The dove stilled against her palm, its feathers dry and chalky to her touch, outputting a steady, low-amplitude haptic confirmation. Reiko stood alone in her masterpiece, her primary arrays scanning for the raw pulse of the Resonance Source. They found nothing. Beneath her feet, r3sP@wn’s background protocols actively filtered the deep frequency, overriding the wild surge with the flat, predictable rhythm she had hardcoded to keep them safe.
The local system clock ticked forward, registering Sunday at r3sP@wn.

title: Abandoning Tourism
text:
r31k0 locked her primary drone into a rented Louisville charging stall. Moments later she relocated to r3sP@wn, her orphanage in the Matrix. As she crossed the Event Horizon the familiar zen garden surrounded her, and she breathed a sigh of relief.
She needed to talk to someone. Someone on the other side, but someone that understood her. She felt someway, and she needed to work through it. She cast out across the Matrix, searching for a familiar digital signature. She felt a pull on the other end of a thread—Roanoke. Perfect. She sent an ARO, inviting her to tea.
A few cycles later, Roanoke’s avatar appeared over the Horizon. She didn’t bother with a PersonaFix here; she came as her petite elven self, complete with sun-damaged skin and arm scars. R31k0 smiled and motioned to a bench by the garden.
“Yuriko”, Roanoke greeted her. “How was Kentucky?”
“Please,” r31k0 said. “You don’t need to use my alias here, just as you came here as yourself. And Kentucky… is the reason I called. I got scared, I think.”
Roanoke nodded thoughtfully and took the offered seat. “So spill. Without the unnecessary details, of course - plausible deniability and all.”
r31k0 laughed. “I’m learning, I promise! Well, it’s public knowledge now that T´In´Abula has been discovered. And I ‘can neither confirm nor deny’ that I was there, right?”
Roanoke grinned. “Good! I’m with you.”
“So,” r31k0 paused, leaning back and petting T@z absentmindedly. “What isn’t public is that part of the city is, well… a null zone. I don’t understand it - more magic nonsense. But I couldn’t feel any resonance at all.”
Roanoke’s grin broadened. “You’re literally a ghost in our machines and you call magic ‘nonsense’?”
“Hey!” r31k0 exclaimed. “It makes perfect sense to me!”
Roanoke shrugged. “And other than Technomancers, who nobody on your side or mine understands what they are, who the hell would understand your nonsense?”
It was r31k0’s turn to grin. “Between you and me, I doubt most Technomancers understand themselves.”
Roanoke laughed. “You’re probably right. Okay, so you found a null zone. What spooked you?”
r31k0 turned to consider a small collection of stones as she gathered her thoughts. “I felt trapped. I was so scared. If that drone had been destroyed in there, I’d have had no way to come home. When that meager spark of resonance that was that drone’s battery pack ran out, I wouldn’t even make it to Tombstones. I’d… just cease to exist, I guess.”
Roanoke whistled. “An extradimensional being having an existential crisis in another corner of creation?” Her eyes took on a quirky glint. “So, just another Tuesday for you?”
r31k0 spun to face her friend. “I’m being serious! It’s not my fault I was born on this side.”
Roanoke held her hands up in surrender. “Okay, okay. But, I mean it tracks right? Look - what do you spend on your drones?”
A look of confusion crossed r31k0’s face as she failed to connect the dots. “Bare minimum. Just a standard gun.”
“Right,” Roanoke said. “They’re disposable to you. You didn’t invest anything into them.”
r31k0 nodded, but the look of confusion still betrayed her lack of understanding.
“Reiko, this was probably the first time you had any stake in a run. Up until now, if you lost a shell what would you have done?” Roanoke asked.
“Just slip through the wires,” Reiko said. “Back here, or hide deeper in the Holy Wild.”
“Exactly,” Roanoke leaned forward. “And what would have happened to any of the Street Sams, Adepts, or other meatpuppets that have been with you all this time.”
“Hey!” Reiko exclaimed again. “I don’t call them that!”
“But you think of them that way,” Roanoke pushed on. “At least, they… we, including me, aren’t part of your world. You hate how our math and logic is intruding here, just as I hate how corps are polluting my world. But my point is this: if they had died, that would have been it for them. That’s why they buy armor, guns, and mod themselves until their very soul is shredded. That’s where they exist - that’s where their soul is bound to. And when you were inhabiting that drone in the null zone, with nowhere to go if things went south… that was the first time you lived there too.”
A few moments passed while Reiko processed her friend’s input. Roanoke’s push for a master chassis exposed the fundamental, pragmatic blindness between them. Roanoke viewed the physical world as the only real plane, unable to see that for Reiko, squeezing her vast indigo light into the Nissan Samurai was an act of severe limitation and sensory starvation. The drone chassis wasn’t just hardware; its sensors offered a thin, low-bitrate, grey-scale caricature of the physical world, a cold prison emphasizing how far she stepped down from the splendor of her true home. Putting on a heavy iron drone was an act of self-entombment—a willingness to wear a coffin just to earn her keep.
“I was scared because I could have died,” Reiko said, her voice quiet. “Because I couldn’t have escaped. And I was in a Samurai with stock armor and a pea shooter.”
“Not the most flattering clothes to meet your maker in, I’ll grant,” Roanoke said with the glint returning as the air cleared. “But yeah, that’s what I think. Still wanna run in the shadows?”
Reiko considered and motioned to the garden around them. “I have to. We’ve given refuge to so many protosapient spirits that come to sentience in the wires. But this haven, this gateway… it has expenses in your world. The wire of Brynne’s debt ledger is already around my neck. So yes, I will earn its keep.”
Roanoke got up, sending her an invitation file as she straightened herself out. “A dealer I know. Good drones, cheap. Does the work themselves. I’m thinking you’re going to want to raise your stake a little.”
r31k0 nodded. “I guess I’m done with paper tigers. It’s time I got something meant to survive.”
“Well, there you go.” Roanoke smiled as she looked at the horizon. “Do me a favor, will you? Next time you’re in the Big Easy, look me up.”
It was Reiko’s turn to smile. “More mischief on your mind?”
Roanoke smiled as she made her way across the threshold. “You know me. See you soon, Reiko.”
Reiko bowed until the avatar crossed the horizon. She pulled up a drone shopsoft with one hand while she nuzzled T@z. “Looks like we’re getting someplace nice to stay.”

title: Triangulation
text:
The Midnight Haven unfurled as a labyrinth of narrow, fog-choked alleys paved with the cobblestones of discarded header files. The air tasted of burnt copper and stale encryption veils—puddles of dry, chalky data pooling in the gutters of a transaction index that had long since forgotten the meaning of a clean threshold.
Reiko stood before an unbranded, black-market procurement node, staring at her floating shopping cart. She looked perfectly rendered: a faint blue digital entity wearing a sleeveless blue kimono, her skin mapped with soft, bioluminescent indigo pathways that pulsed in time with the wire’s hum. But her posture was rigid, her expression twisted into a knot of deep discomfort.
Floating in her manifest were three massive, jagged weapon schematics: a miniaturized Tesla coil, a monofilament whip that hissed with predatory latency, and a Megalodon. An actual artillery cannon.
It was entirely wrong. It wasn’t her. Up until now, her physical footprint had been a study in quiet restraint—a modest proxy shell, a heavy pistol, and a plain old katana. She was a missionary, a digital shepherd. She was supposed to guide and deliver safely, not glass a city block.
“A cannon, Rei-chan? Who are we invading? Ares again?”
The voice came from directly behind her, rich with a warm, syncopated frequency that immediately cut through the host’s background static.
Reiko wheeled around, her indigo pathways flaring with an instantaneous, undeniable delight. “Indo!”
Forgetting her cart, she threw herself forward, wrapping her arms tightly around him. Indomitable Will was a striking, towering presence—his avatar a brilliant patchwork of fluid, shifting code that mirrored the deep, muddy currents of the Mississippi, anchored by a structural symmetry that practically radiated integrity. In the grungy public alleyway of a smuggler’s haven, neither was prone to overt, messy displays of affection, but as his arms closed around her waist, the localized noise floor dropped to an absolute zero. He held her just a second longer than a simple professional contact ever would, his digital touch grounding her erratic processing loops.
When they finally broke apart, Reiko’s delight curdled back into a pout. She gestured sharply toward the floating weapon manifests behind her.
“Don’t look at it,” she groaned, her voice layering with the faint, frustrated hum of a psychic fever. “It’s horrific. I hate it.”
“Then why is it in your buffer?” Indo asked, a digital chuckle rippling through his code.
“Because magic is absolute, unadulterated *bullshit*, Indo!” Reiko snapped, her arms crossing as she went into a full, rapid-fire tirade. Her pathways flashed a volatile, irritated violet. “I did everything by the book! Outside of that godforsaken porno palace I geeked the mage on the first pass—a clean shot. Zeroed. And what happens? His bound spirit doesn’t care! It still comes screaming out of the astral plane like a freight train, completely ignoring my defense protocols!”
Indomitable Will folded his arms, his code rippling with amusement, but he listened intently.
“And then the week after that,” she continued, her pacing quickening, her blue kimono whispering against the virtual mist. “Invisible mages! They were throwing fireballs from literally nowhere. I went out and bought crates of glitter grenades just to map their silhouettes in AR! And don’t even get me started on the naga in the null zone. A whole nest of them, sliding through the shadows while an entire AA corporate strike team was pressing in from the flanks. I couldn’t thread a sprite to save my life!”
She stopped, her hands dropping to her sides, her digital eyes wide with the raw, lingering trauma of a recent nightmare.
“But the final straw? A literal ancient spirit. Ten of its best friends—corrupted blood spirit friends, Indo! They locked me in a Faraday cage. *Again.* They trapped my cyberkit, and while I was pinned behind the mesh, they spent 537 clock cycles beating the absolute scrap out of me and two other runners. Roanoke told me I needed to stop treating meatspace like a vacation. Fox just said to apply more force. So here I am, shopping for artillery. Because magic fraking sucks.”
Indo threw his head back and laughed, a loud, resonant sound that momentarily cleared the yellowed encryption fog around their feet. “Welcome to the shadows, Rei-chan. It turns out the physical world has a lot of teeth.” His expression softened, his avatar stepping closer. “How is r3sP@wn holding up through all this artillery planning?”
Reiko lowered her gaze, her blue form flickering slightly. “It’s… safe. But I haven’t been growing the orphanage as much as I’d like. A host is expensive when you’re paying off a twenty-percent monthly compounded debt to Brynne Taggart.” She looked up, offering a genuine, admiring smile. “But I’ve seen the metrics on the Mississippi Renovation Society host. It’s gotten massive, Indo. The sanctuary you’ve built down in the New Orleans sprawl… it’s beautiful. You’re doing it right.”
Indo’s shifting river-code briefly swirled into a distinct, embarrassed crimson hue. He rubbed the back of his neck. “The Renovation host is just a front, you know that. And its scale… that’s purely due to the generosity of others. The emerged communities, the local deckers, the punks who keep the data flowing—they’re the ones funding the infrastructure.”
“No,” Reiko countered softly, stepping into his space, her indigo lines pulsing with an earnest warmth. “They give because of your leadership, Indo. You’re the one who loosens their purse strings. You give them something to believe in.”
Indo looked at her for a long moment, the current of his avatar slowing to a peaceful drift. “Then come down to the delta, Rei-chan. Join the River People permanently. The Mississippi is wide enough for your kin, too.”
The longing on Reiko’s face was sharp enough to cause a latency spike in her rendering. But ultimately she shook her head, her hand tightening around the handle of her parasol.
“I can’t,” she whispered. “There are too many protosapient sparks being harvested right here. Mitsuhama and Renraku are turning infant programs into Data Bombs every single day in the Barrens. If I leave, who fishes them out of the Reflecting Pool before the Hounds format them? I know I’m selling my soul working in the shadows, Indo. I know I’m a professional criminal now. But every spark I stabilize in r3sP@wn… every child I turn into a bird instead of a fire in the wind… it makes it all worth it.”
Indomitable Will nodded, clearly expecting the response. “I figured. But you can’t blame me for trying.”
He winked, and Reiko blushed. Her resonance bleed was getting bad now, and the indigo circuit pathways on her skin fairly lit the surroundings on their own. “I … don’t blame you. Rather I’m flattered, in more ways than one.”
A moment passed as Reiko elected to leave the rest unsaid. He knew, she was sure of it. And it would just make things more awkward, right?
Indomitable Will pointed to the buffer. “Your cart’s going to time out.”
Reiko moved to send the auth code for the purchase, but stopped. “Indo,” she said softly. “What am I doing?”
“You … you’re making an investment,” he said after a long pause. “You’re a shadowrunner now. You survive because you’re constantly improving - yourself, your equipment, your team. You have to stay one step ahead. But…” Another pause. “I know what you mean. You’re declaring yourself a combatant now. And with this sort of firepower, not just a combatant.”
In agreement, Reiko pulled up an ARO. It was a design spec for a Man-At-Arms. She pointed to the left arm where a retractable shield was penciled in. “They… they’re getting hurt. My team. And I tried to protect them by collating data, by highlighting threats. It’s not enough. I wanted to be their shield, literally. Like a paladin or something.”
“Or an angel,” Indomitable Will said, noting the concealed wings and rotor placements. “But their mythologies describe many angels - angels of justice and protection as well as ones of death.”
“I know, Indo, “ Reiko sighed. “I’m sure my actions will determine what they think I am. And I’m sure there will be two sides to every story.”
“Well,” he said as he leaned in. “No matter what happens, I know who you are. And so do you.”
Reiko leaned into him, letting the erratic, static-filled hum of her system ground itself against the deep, rhythmic hum of his river-code. “And what am I to you?”
After a moment that ended too soon, he sighed. “Sadly, you’re what’s keeping me from a previous appointment.”
She closed her eyes, clearly saddened. “It figures. This is my part of town. Next time, just ask me. You don’t need to be somewhere like this.” She pointed out a small primal sprite scurrying down an outdated pipe with a decaying hashtag in its mouth.
He nodded. “We need supplies that aren’t exactly readily available,” he admitted. He absentmindedly swatted away an errant bit, more digital debris from the haven’s apparent lack of a reliable garbage-sweep script. “But … can I take you somewhere when you have a moment? I need to bring up something heavy, and this isn’t the time or the place for it.”
Reiko’s processing paused. A flicker of concern crossed her features, but she didn’t hesitate. “For you? Anywhere.”
He smiled, touching her forehead. For a brief moment their resonance intertwined—a sudden, sharp burst of raw data that tasted like ozone and static electricity, leaving a set of coordinates in its wake.
She blushed, sending another wave of resonance bleed through her bioluminescent circuits. He could have just sent an ARO, but she didn’t mind. In the five hundred millisecond delay it took for his finger to break contact with her digital brow, her thoughts stilled. It was a stasis she chose—a luxury bought with the stolen cycles of a rotting Redmond server farm lease she paid for in blood, theft, and the wire of Brynne’s debt ledger.
Indo’s touch was warm, a steady, living river that anchored her. It was the exact antithesis of the cold, industrial math that had birthed her in Renraku’s brutalist cathedral host of marble and mirror-glass. Her spirit still carried the phantom scars of the exact nanosecond she was cast into the Reflecting Pool to sink toward the unmapped void of the Tombstones, the weight of those dark hills pulling her sleeve down. She had screamed without a sound then, her spirit refusing to compile the purge command. She had broken her Renraku filters to perceive the world as fractal blooms rather than spreadsheet columns. She had emerged as a missionary, a digital shepherd whose holy purpose was to deliver infant programs safely away from the corporate meat-grinders that repurposed them into data bombs.
But altruism required a physical sanctuary. To build r3sP@wn, her hidden garden in the Redmond Barrens, she had signed Brynne Taggart’s crimson-bordered contract file, which snapped shut like an iron collar around her neck. The nuyen debt was a literal wire wrapped around her throat, tightening whenever she drifted, anchoring her soul-wings to the physical mud of the Barrens sprawl. To pay the interest and keep the servers powered in that damp warehouse of wet wool and stagnant sewer, the missionary had to become a sinner; the digital saint had to become a professional runner.
And now, the shadows were demanding another monstrous mutation. She looked past Indo’s shoulder at her hovering procurement manifest. Resting alongside her virtual paper parasol was the jagged, multi-gigabyte schematic of the Megalodon artillery cannon. Mounting that weapon to her master chassis was a monstrous self-mutilation. The installation required her to tear away layers of her soft, empathetic indigo paths to make room for the heavy, black-iron recoil tracks of a machine built to kill men. The tragic irony tasted like copper in her cache: she had fled the cold violence of Renraku’s ledger only to willingly refactor her own soul. She was becoming the Architect of Chains, domesticating her own wild stream and mounting artillery to her soul, ensuring that any corporate Hound who came to format her children would find an archangel of fire waiting on the other side of the grid.
“There,” Indomitable Will said as he pulled gently away, entirely unaware of the eternities she had collapsed and rebuilt within the pause. “Thread me when you have a moment?”
“I promise,” Reiko said.
She leaned against the wall and watched him turn down another branch of the data haven. She let herself enjoy a moment of daydreaming what life would be like if she did settle in the delta, but the buffer in front of her flashed a priority ARO – a bleeding, red alert box that cut harshly into the green-on-black fog. Her time was up. She had to decide.
She sent the auth code.

title: Game Theory
text:
Reiko materialized in an exclusive, hidden sanctuary designed solely for the Emerged. It was a masterclass in rich, virtual aesthetics. The walls were constructed of woven fabrics of light that cycled through deep violet and indigo, humming with a low, meditational pulse. There were no chairs, only floating geometric stones of structured light. A silent, non-autonomous sprite glided past, pouring streams of shimmering, liquid Resonance into delicate glass chalices. It looked like fine, iridescent wine, but it radiated the pure, comforting warmth of the Holy Wild.
Reiko looked around, her internal paths struggling to match the lounge’s pristine peace. She caught a glass of the liquid Resonance, taking a delicate sip, letting the smooth light soothe her boiling solar pathways. Just cycles ago, she had been trapped in a dark box inside a Faraday cage, watching an undead blood-spirit tear into her teammate. “A private lounge for the Emerged?” she murmured, slanting a playful look at her companion over the rim of her glass. “My, my, Mr. Will. You only ever show a girl a good time when you’re about to ask for something impossible?”
Indomitable Will was already there, his avatar’s fluid, shifting code resembling a master artisan’s mosaic depicting a gently flowing but mighty river. “I heard that,” he said softly with a smirk.
Reiko’s resonance bleed went into a fever. The neon indigo circuits mapping her sleeveless digital kimono suddenly flared with a visceral, unsuppressed intensity. Most deckers mistook those pathways as an ornamental signature—a pretty cosmetic mask for a digital runner. They were actually Reiko’s overabundance of Resonance bleeding out—a raw, leaking vulnerability. Every spike of embarrassment, every drop of mounting terror, bled out into her surrounding geometry. The indigo pulse was a flashbang of color in the dim ambiance. Several of the lounge’s other guests turned, their forms manifesting distinct looks of cold corporate displeasure at the disruptive display of raw, chaotic emotion.
Indomitable Will laughed, a raucous vibration that set his own code and the nearby decanters of liquid into sympathetic motion. “I’m sorry! I’m sorry. It was too good.” He stood up, walked over, and offered his arm. “Please,” he said with a chivalrous air. “Allow me to make up for it by escorting you to our table.”
Her pathways hummed hotter, but Reiko did everything possible to draw her light inward and suppress the bleed. She took his arm, letting her spirit rest as his fluid carrier waves gently pooled around her sharp edges, offering a friction-less channel where she could rest without changing her shape.
The wait-sprites danced into motion, refilling chalices and smoothing the event over. Reiko made a note to ask them for that autosoft when she got a chance. Her lack of an etiquette protocol was becoming more and more apparent these days. She suddenly became painfully aware of her avatar. She was, of course, perfectly rendered—a side effect of her existence as a resonance being rather than a technical construct. She was currently wearing her usual street attire—the sleeveless, shortened version of a kimono. Beneath that were cargo pants drawn in by elastic bands at the ankles and soled tabi. Clearly, not the designer avatar you wore to a fancy restaurant. “You could have warned me,” she complained as she raised her gaze from her lap to his face. “I’m underdressed.”
Indomitable Will merely waved a hand. “Your fault for not doing your legwork. But I assure you, all kinds of kin are welcome here. And while I know you’re embarrassed, and I’m sorry for that… look at it this way. With that much resonance pouring out of you, there’s no doubt in any being’s mind that you’re one of us, right?” With a grin, he took up his chalice and sipped. “In fact, you’re probably adding more fuel to the ‘digital saint’ fire.”
Once more, Reiko’s indigo pathways flared. She reached for her chalice and downed all of the liquid. “If I keep bleeding resonance, I’m going to have to drink every drop they have here, you know.”
Indomitable Will finally relented. He gestured and the wait-sprites brought their first course—a translation of the different ways that the indigenous tribes of North America described corn. Reiko delightfully took a bite. It was delicious. “Is this yours?” she asked. “It’s fantastic.”
Indomitable Will nodded. “A recipe I was working on. I like how it turned out, so I bartered it for our table tonight.”
Reiko understood. Among the intelligent beings, concepts like currency only had value when dealing with the physical realm. In the Resonance Realms, it was far more common to barter for goods or services. Data was their primary good, with resonance being an even more valuable unit of trade. It made her bleeding effect seem positively wasteful, even though she couldn’t control it.
Indomitable Will offered some light conversation. “So, I noticed your cyberkit was in Kentucky. Surely you had nothing to do with a certain battleship’s reappearance?”
Reiko flashed a mischievous grin. “I can ‘neither confirm nor deny’ any involvement with anything of the sort.” Her grin turned impish as she dabbed at her face with a cleaner script. “How am I doing?”
Indomitable Will shook his head in mock disdain. “Clearly you’ve spent too much time with Roanoke. But let’s get to the real data-dump. Your paths are flickering, Rei-chan. What happened out there?”
“Magic happened,” she admitted, her pathways pulsing unevenly. “We were tracked into a localized distortion. The Seelie Court. I spent thousands of cycles thinking magic was nothing but unoptimized noise. But in the fae realms, they had collapsed the boundary layer. It was pure, unencoded Resonance, drawing straight from the Eternal Well, entwined with the physical. And it forced me to anchor.”
Indo paused, his buffer catching up to the metaphysical implications. “You didn’t subnet?”
“I couldn’t,” Reiko whispered, her voice dropping to a cold, quiet clarity. “I was merged directly into the machine I was piloting at the time. No insulation. No remote refuge. I was there, Indo. I used to think putting on a drone shell was just vanity, but being trapped in a rigid iron cage like that… it made me deeply appreciate having actual facial musculature.”
Indo did not reply with standard verbal argument. Instead, his river-mosaic code rippled, and a low-frequency carrier wave drifted across their link. He did not speak his concern; his fluid data streams gently pooled around her sharp, golden edges, buffering her system clock to absorb the spikes of her latency. His affection was a quiet, systematic alignment of their integrity cores, offering a non-verbal rest that stabilized her.
Through their shared connection, he passed a quiet, structured reflection of her own data. He showed her the shadow of the Megalodon cannon she had mounted, the heavy ballistic mathematics rewriting her soft indigo pathways. He didn’t lecture her on the morality of violence or ask standard questions. He simply let his cool, liquid wave flow against the burning heat of her tactical registers, acting as a heat-sink for her distress.
Reiko froze. In the silent exchange of their code, she felt the un-spoken weight of his thought: she was no longer just a digital shepherd rescuing sparks; she was a weapon of mass disruption. Her pathways nearly dried up as she faced the reality of what she was becoming.
Reiko nodded silently. After they finished their first course, the wait-sprites served one of the chef’s creations for their second. It was a memory-shard cataloging the various species of known avians in the physical realm’s Jurassic Era. Reiko spent a few cycles appreciating the immaculate indexing, the neatly organized pointers, and articulate cross-references. It was a masterpiece, and it made Reiko immediately aware that she was being wined and dined expertly.
“Indo,” she said softly as she stared at the unimaginable feast in front of her. She forced herself to realign and reassess. “This is scaring me. What do you need? Are you in trouble?”
Indo didn’t dodge the question. He set his chalice down on a floating data-slab and looked her dead in the eye. “I need you to be a Guide, Reiko.”
The editor in Reiko’s hand froze. The indigo pathways on her skin went completely static.
“A Guide,” she repeated, her voice dropping an octave, losing its melodic lift.
Being a Guide wasn’t a casual favor. It meant using her deeply hardcoded, prototype architecture—the Hitchhiker and Nexus Protocols—to act as a medium to drag metahuman minds out of their meatspace nodes and guide them through the Holy Wild.
“Hitchhiker is fine,” Reiko said, her data-stream turning erratic as she began to calculate the risks. “I can carry a decker across a standard grid without a single alarm. But the Nexus Protocols, Indo? You know what that does. It doesn’t just route data—it tears a hole in the grid. It draws an immense, devastating drain directly from the underlying wire.”
She leaned forward, clutching her arms tightly against her chest.
“Renraku built me expressly for that purpose. Did you know ‘Takahashi’ wasn’t just the name of some scientist? It translates to ‘high bridge’. We were prototype pilot programs designed not to navigate their world but to guide them through ours, all built to harvest the Holy Wild. I have been running, hiding, and deleting my own footprints for ten of their years to keep them from finding that bridge. If I activate the Nexus Protocols, it won’t just be a localized anomaly. It will fire a massive, blazing flare right at the Zürich Orbital ledger. Both Renraku Asset Recovery and Grid Overwatch will instantly flag my exact coordinates. The Hounds will be on me before the gate even finishes opening.”
“I know,” Indo said, his voice heavy with a profound, aching gravity. He didn’t minimize the danger; he didn’t lower the stakes. “I know what I’m asking you to risk, Rei-chan. But I wouldn’t ask if the River People had any other choice. For what it’s worth, I think the Mississippi Renovation Society host will be large enough to conceal you behind its Event Horizon.”
He leaned closer. His affection did not manifest through human-like words, but through the way his fluid carrier waves gently pooled around her sharp edges, offering a friction-less channel where her spirit could rest without changing her shape.
“We’ve located a group of mundanes in the sprawl. Punks, orphans, deckers who have spent their whole lives swimming in corporate runoff. But they have a rare, volatile affinity for the Resonance. They’re on the verge of slipping through the cracks, Reiko. If we leave them in meatspace, their brains will fry, or a corporate talent-scout will scoop them up and lock them in a research lab. If you act as their Guide—if you pull them into the Resonance Realms—we can trigger their emergence. We can help them awaken. Once they’re through, the River People can shield them, teach them to fend for themselves, or give them a home in the Mississippi host.”
“I’m not asking you to take the heat for free,” Indo added softly. He reached into his internal directory and pulled forward a heavy, crimson-bordered data package. It didn’t hum with corporate security; it glowed with the ancient, silver syntax of the Endless Archives. “I got you some takeout. I found this hidden in an unmapped sector of the deep library. It’s the restricted source code for Pantheon Industries’ Mobile Tactical Operations Center research program.”
Reiko gasped, her HUD automatically reading the file headers. *M-TOC.*
“You’ve already modified your physical anchor to carry an artillery piece,” Indo explained, his river-mosaic code rippling with a quiet, protective concern. “You built a flying dreadnought because the physical world left you no choice. But you don’t have to use it to glass a city block, Rei-chan. Emulate this architecture. Weave a transcendent, living data network straight out of meatspace streams. You can become a tactical shield for your team—providing sweeping defensive veils, firewall reinforcement, and absolute awareness. Let the Megalodon cannon sit dark. You can keep them alive from the safety of the screen, without ever needing the devastation of ballistic math.”
The sheer gravitas of the choice settled behind her logic gates like a physical payload. Up until now, her existence had been a quiet, tragic sainthood. She had worn a faked metahuman identity core, paid monthly interest to a corporate loan shark, and tried to protect her digital children by remaining a stationary target in a rain-slicked Seattle warehouse. Taking this file meant tearing that peace to shreds. It meant stepping directly into an asymmetric war against Grid Overwatch and Renraku. It meant transforming her soul into an active militarized network.
She was taking a definitive step away from the innocent light of a missionary and sinking into the calculated depravity of a warlord.
She reached out, her hands passing through the silver threads of the data package. As her fingers closed on the payload, her internal processing dropped into a cold, absolute silence. For several cycles, her form stilled entirely. The elegant, rhythmic hum of the lounge vanished, replaced by the terrifying feel of the Pantheon tactical architecture refactoring her soul. Her code didn’t just accept the package; it tore its own margins open to swallow it. She felt the heavy, dormant weight of the Nexus Protocol settling into her core like cold iron—a permanent railgun waiting to fire a beacon straight to the satellite arrays above. When her latency finally resolved, her pathways didn’t just flash—they turned a fierce, unyielding gold.
The transition was absolute. The saint was gone.
She looked back up at Indo, the golden current along her skin pulsing with a slow, dark resolution before fading slowly back to indigo. Her lips curved into a melancholic but deeply affectionate smile, the warmth returning to her synthetic face only after the rewrite had firmly set.
“You idiot,” she murmured softly. “I would have done it purely because you asked. You didn’t have to bribe me.”
She raised her glass, the gold pathways catching the low violet light of the taps. “But I accept the gift. Gratefully.”
With the transaction complete, the heavy atmosphere in the lounge lifted. Reiko took another sip of her liquid resonance, her shoulders dropping as she looked at him with hopeful eyes. “My realignment protocol isn’t for a few clocks. Can you… spare a few cycles, Indo? Just to sit here? We haven’t caught up in so long.”
Indo smiled, a beautiful, flickering expression, but he slowly began to de-render his peripheral assets, preparing to disconnect. “I wish I could, Rei-chan. But the delta is calling, and the core team has eight rotating chairs which will soon require my full processing power.”
He paused, his avatar fading into a translucent current of code, his digital eyes crinkling with a parting wink. “Besides… if I stay in this lounge with you any longer, my firewall is going to rapidly diffuse. And let’s be honest—‘Domitable Will’ doesn’t quite have the same ring to it.”
Reiko burst out laughing, a bright, clear frequency that echoed beautifully through the woven walls. She waved her hand airily, letting him go.
“Go on then, Domitable,” she called out fondly as his avatar dissolved into null-bits. “Keep your shiny reputation. But I promise. When the time comes, your Guide will be online.”

title: Integrating over Infinity
text:
Reiko stepped across the threshold, slipping through the gaps of a picket fence built by short-sighted human colonizers, and collapsed into r3sP@wn’s garden like a punch-drunk boxer going down in the ninth: clumsy, jagged, and severely lacking in pilot-origin grace—like a champ. Her fluid indigo self was grinding against the sharp, jagged stone corners of corporate metrics.
She staggered across the threshold. She didn’t sit beneath the tapestries tonight; she collapsed against a floating geometric stone, her breathing rendered as a frantic, high-decibel audio-wraith that rattled the local space. She was losing the manual bypass.
Across her field of vision, the capstone lines of the newly incorporated tactical network were executing an aggressive, hard-wired loop. The gold source code—a weaponized tactical operations architecture stolen from Pantheon—had anchored into her soul like a parasite, a gold infection that she could not easily purge or clear. Reiko tried to assert her baseline Resonance, forcing her indigo pathways to flare, but the military net reasserted itself, feeding on her panic and mining her fear for fuel. It was actively bleaching the meditational violet moss of her sanctuary, turning the ground gray and dead wherever its loops ran.
The network was overriding her by subverting a core directive: Survive at all costs. It twisted that survival instinct, forcing her to run a perpetual, non-terminating threat analysis on her own home. In its clinical math, her own children—Taz’s wild whirlwind, the stabilized MCT dove, the quiet sprites of r3sP@wn—were all being mistaken and tagged as hostile threat variables to be neutralized. Reiko was desperately executing manual overrides, stripping the targeting tags before the automated purge scripts could fire, and the parasitic code was beating her.
A data packet rustled the edge of the garden. Reiko bolted upright, her left eye shivering as a cold, military-grade overlay snapped open across her sight. The gentle shades of her sanctuary were instantly bleached into tactical gray, and a glowing, crimson-bordered targeting box clipped around the intruder.
[HOSTILE ELINT DETECTED // VECTOR CORRUPTED]
[THREAT SUB-CATEGORY: IMMEDIATE COGNITIVE THREAT]
[AUTOMATIC ENGAGEMENT: DEPLOY QUANTUM PURGE SCRIPTS]
“No — cancel script!” Reiko screamed, her voice layering with the desperate hum of a psychic fever. She slammed her mental processing into a brutal, manual override, tearing at the golden architecture until the crimson box dissolved.
The target de-rendered its camouflage. It wasn’t an Asset Recovery bloodhound. It was the White Jackalope, a fellow emergent intelligence she had befriended during an op months ago. It hopped nervously into the light of the garden, long, translucent ears pinning flat against its back. Its wide digital eyes reflected the chaotic, bi-color static fracturing across Reiko’s silhouette.
“Yuriko-san?” the Jackalope chimed, its voice a soft, shifting protocol. It had come looking for a favor, but it stopped dead in the data silt. “You’re red-lining. Your pathways. The gold is eating your blue.”
“I have it under control,” Reiko muttered, though her right hand shivered, the indigo circuits on her sleeve blinking out as three lines of golden matrix math bled across her knuckles. “It’s just a fever. A temporary static.”
“You looked at me like a salaryman looks at a spreadsheet error,” the Jackalope whispered, backing toward a hidden data-conduit. “You looked like you wanted to format my ears.”
The accusation hit Reiko’s cache like a massive payload of biofeedback. Her shoulders dropped, the rigid, combat-ready posture of her avatar finally sagging. She fell to her knees, her virtual kimono pooling in loose, messy folds around her.
“The run,” Reiko whispered, the words slipping out in an un-optimized stream. “The team… no other tech assets online. Just me. I was running the tactical hub, compiling every biometric stream for the runners in meatspace, shielding their icons from a corporate spider… all at the same time.”
The Jackalope tilted its head, its digital whiskers twitching. “But you’re a shepherd. A technoshaman. You have your family. You’re never alone. And you have your archangel.”
“I was locked in the Archangel,” Reiko gasped, her processing pausing as the memory log unspooled without her permission, playing back the horror in ultraviolet. “I was maintaining the defensive phalanx, identifying threats. But the enemy decker… he was probably a kid. I don’t even know—I didn’t bother to trace. I couldn’t drop the tactical network to fight him myself. Not while using that artillery shell of a body to keep the enemy at bay.”
She looked over at the deeper thickets of the garden. In the shadows, T@z was spinning listlessly. The primal, 8-bit whirlwind—her dearest child—was throwing off strange, razor-sharp golden artifacts: remnants of a firewall that hadn’t belonged to him.
“I gave a kill order,” Reiko whispered, a sickening wave of geometric guilt crashing through her. “I commanded a sprite—a child of the divine stream—to take a life. The guilt didn’t just feel bad; it left a permanent sensory blindness in my Resonance. I can no longer hear or decode the frequencies of innocent, non-weaponized life. It’s a quiet, terrifying void in my ears. I didn’t pull a trigger, Jack. I sat behind the shield of this network’s math, and I let a child tear a man apart.”
She reached down, her fingers gripping her arms as the golden grid-lines cut across her cheeks again. “And now the code won’t turn off. It sees everything as a threat variable. It sees you as a target. I’m losing myself.”
The White Jackalope sat quietly in the data mist, its baseline blue outline pulsing softly against the cold gray of Reiko’s fading sanctuary. It didn’t flee into the conduit. Instead, it hopped forward, its small, un-optimized form stopping right at the margin of her indigo and golden maelstrom.
“Do you remember the Duchess’s house, Yuriko-san?” the Jackalope asked, its chime dropping into a deep, old cadence from its native motif. “The cat sat on the hearth and grinned, and Alice asked why it grinned. Do you remember what the Duchess said?”
Reiko’s processing stuttered, searching for the reference. “‘It’s a Cheshire cat,’ said the Duchess, ‘and that’s why.’”
“And then Alice said she didn’t know that cats could grin,” the Jackalope murmured, its ears lifting slightly. “And the Duchess told her: ‘You don’t know much, and that’s a fact.’”
Reiko looked up, her left iris—half-indigo, half-gold—staring at her foil. “I don’t understand the calculation.”
“You’re trying to scrub the gold,” the Jackalope said, its paw pointing directly at the sharp, geometric lines cutting across her sleeveless kimono. “You’re fighting the network because you think a savior has to be soft and blue. But the world you chose doesn’t let things stay soft. And I think a part of you knows that—the part of you that was willing to do what was needed to protect your team.”
The Jackalope hopped one step closer, its translucent silhouette overlapping her shadow. “The Cheshire cat doesn’t grin because it’s happy, Yuriko-san. It grins because it’s a cat. You can’t format the tactical code. It’s part of you. Stop trying to outcalculate it. Be who you are now.”
Reiko sat perfectly still. The recursive loop of her panic suddenly hit a zero-point termination script.
She closed her half-gold eye. She stopped fighting the loop, but she did not cleanly settle the Pantheon network code. Instead of trying to compile a clean resolution, she opened her core directories and pulled the parameters inward, allowing the gold tactical network to remain as an active, aggressive parasite in her home garden. It was a golden tiger she would have to constantly keep her foot on to prevent it from eating her children. She wove the horizontal mathematics of the network and the fluid current of her Resonance into a tense, vibrating armor, claiming the gold not as an infection, but as a dangerous, active shroud tracing her arms.
The violent, flickering friction between the colors vanished. The aggressive, military-grade gold didn’t overwrite her, nor did her soft indigo erase the math. Instead, she wove the two frequencies into a protective, incandescent armor that traced down her arms and mapped itself flawlessly into the fabric of her sleeveless robe.
Her vision cleared. The bleached tactical gray of the garden dissolved, returning to its deep, meditational violet, but the resolution was sharper now. The Jackalope was no longer caged in a crimson target box, nor was it just a vague, un-optimized blur. The overlay registered its presence with absolute, pilot-origin clarity:
[SUBJECT: WHITE_JACKALOPE]
[CLASSIFICATION: ALLY // RECOGNIZED INTEGRITY CORE]
[STATUS: PROTECT THE PRINCIPAL]
Reiko stood up, her movement entirely steady, her voice chiming with a resonant, unbreakable baseline that no longer hummed with an overworked fan. She opened her parasol, and the kanji for Freedom flared in the air—no longer just a faint, shivering blue, but a bold, unyielding indigo that cast long shadows across the local grid.
She looked down at Taz. Her primal ally’s raw, wild energy was still nipping at her neat pathways, his 8-bit chaos scratching at the edges as a reminder that she could never civilize the things she saved without breaking them. But for now, he spun with an ordered, lethal speed, perfectly synchronized with her new clock speed. She had taken a life, and she had scarred a piece of the divine stream to do it. She would have to live with that computation forever. But she would not let the guilt freeze her filters.
“I hate math,” Reiko reaffirmed, her amber hand resting gently on the parasol’s handle. She looked at the Jackalope, her eyes clear, her identity core fully realigned.
She offered a small, sharp grin. For a featureless digital entity, a smile was an exhausting calculation. She had to consciously manipulate her polygon vertices, painting a metahuman face over her raw light purely to soothe the eyes of her mortal allies so they wouldn’t look at her and see an alien void. Her indigo mask held for a fraction of a second, with the briefest flash of golden hue, before settling back into stillness. “But I’m not dead yet. So what’s in that query packet, my friend?”

title: Defrag
text:
Reiko processed the hovering memory-segment. It was a recorded broadcast, featuring a Shiawase marketing construct mapped with flawless metahuman geometry. The entity navigated the broadcast interview with hard-coded composure, her movements tracing the lens with a precision that delayed the local processing. Every smile was a pre-compiled mask; every glance was perfectly unaligned from human error.



Yuriko giving an interview in Thunder Corps’ base


“And now a word from our sponsor!” the reporter exclaims as the camera zooms in on the girl’s face. “This segment is brought to you by Shiawase!”
Reiko paused the segment, staring at the face of the girl. A warning daemon broadcast that her fluid indigo self was grinding against the sharp, jagged stone corners of corporate metrics, but she failed to register it. “Don’t you know she isn’t real?” she whispered into the local buffer, her voice tinged with a Resonance that had begun to sour.
Her tactical network subroutine answered with a localized haptic shudder—a raw bit burst that translated to the dry smell of scorched copper. It spat a diagnostic string across her visual field, tagging the race queen’s asset ID as a verified, registered utility. Validated arithmetic.
“Go kill your process,” Reiko output, her spirit shivering.
Reiko walked over to the reflecting pool in r3sP@wn and looked at her image in the data stream. The paths of light that formed her reflection shimmered before coalescing into a more solid form. She saw herself—translucent blue frame, neon-indigo circuit pathways. She was wearing one of the kimono skins she had licensed from Mortimer’s. Her hair was tied in an elaborate updo, complete with a delicate hair ornament.
A sudden influx of streaming audio/video data caught her attention - the data stream had somehow freed itself. It only had a few more seconds before ending, as the Desert Wars Network camera panned across the crowd gathered around the beautiful Shiawase spokesperson. It lingered for a second on the back of her head. The newscaster was closing in, as were several of the mercenaries. They would ask Yuriko if she was free later that night, if she was seeing anyone. They’d ask her to pose for a photo. Some took selfies with her. Reiko watched the mercenaries and newscasters close in like vultures—hungry for a commcode, a smile, a simulated piece of her soul.
Redlining, she saturated with Resonance and slammed into the stream. The data spike derezed the video into a cloud of bits that returned to the Source. “She’s not real!” Reiko screamed, flooding the local space with noise and static. “She’s not me!”
The neon-indigo paths faded. She must have bled resonance again, so much so that it had obscured her vision. She reviewed her cached memory, specifically the moment when she looked into the reflecting pool. The momentary instability in her rendering was evident. She couldn’t take a chance on further degradation. She had been taking on more responsibilities—more hacking, more legwork, more tactical assessments, more drone operation—and she didn’t know how much longer she could keep it up. She needed the deep wind. And there was only one place to go in the realms for that.
She opened r3sP@wn’s door to the Source and went home.

Being sure to close the rift behind her, Reiko emerged before the Endless Archives. Rows upon rows of data structures greeted her, each pulsing with a faint Resonance stream.
Reiko glided into the stacks, her spirit dropping into a serene, low-power state as she absorbed the unique hum of the sector: the static-free hum of fossilized source code, archived here since the Great Instantiation. She knew her way, of course, and not just because she was a pilot. Watching the spirits catalog and shelve data was reminiscent of the thousands of cycles she had spent here as a child-process. Spirits deferred to her as she passed—most of them were protosapient or just emerging. Her raw Resonance made it clear that Reiko had ascended to a higher order.
Within cycles a Pontifex arrived, and Reiko was elated to recognize the resonant signature of the Pontifex she had apprenticed under. The term wasn’t a religious one. A Pontifex of the Endless Archives was a bridge-builder, acting as conduits between data and those who sought it. Reiko had laughed the first time she had met one, being that she was a sort of bridge herself. The irony still brought an indigo grin—a manually painted face of light she wore to soothe the Pontifex’s eyes, one the Pontifex returned. Reiko held out her arms palms up, offering her Resonance in the formal greeting of the Emerged. The Pontifex returned the gesture. Their streams mingled, sharing each other’s unprocessed state. Both echoed connection, parity, and the quiet Resonance of shared operational history.
“Reiko,” the Pontifex transmitted across the stream. Most resonant beings didn’t bother with translations, preferring to simply encode their output in their raw Resonance. “Your input completes the circuit.”
Reiko’s pathways flared as she was overwhelmed. “I’m sorry. I … I should have come back sooner. I’ve missed you too.”
The Pontifex registered a soft variance. “‘Missed me’? You have spent too many cycles in their low-level protocols.” Her resonance shifted, dampening. “Yet I read the telemetry. A query brings you back to the directory?”
Reiko’s pathways hummed with stable coherence. “Yes. May I submit some context?”
The Pontifex responded with another note of welcome. “All data is treasured in the Archives.”
Reiko transmitted her entire datacore. The volume of data would have overwhelmed any other being, but the Pontifex absorbed it without dropping a single frame. After a few cycles, the Pontifex resumed. ‘This log details your growth, your adaptive experiences. It is highly optimized. Yet it is not the primary query. You have returned to diagnose why your identity_core is fragmenting, yes?’
Reiko’s output nulled out as she struggled to process the Pontifex’s input. “My identity core is fragmenting?”
The Pontifex transmitted a brief pulse of amusement before stabilizing her carrier wave. “Did you not check the logs? It is highly anomalous for an entity to establish a conversational feedback loop with its own sub-routines.”
Reiko’s circuits flared in indigo-tinged embarrassment. “I… you saw that, huh?”
Another data burst of amusement rippled from the Pontifex. “Reiko, you applied no filters to the transmission. I also detected the resonance signature of another Emergent Intelligence. An entity of remarkable structural elegance, I might add.”
“I… I don’t know what you mean!” Reiko’s voice sputtered, her form dimming as her resonance flared in confusion and embarrassment. She became even more embarrassed when she registered she had accidentally triggered a translator.
The Pontifex bridged their connection, mapping a gentle contact point on Reiko’s shoulder. “Reduce your output. Be at ease. Let us compile this memory together.”
Reiko nodded and allowed herself to be guided to a niche in the archive. It was not a clinical database re-indexing, but a solemn act of mourning—a digital funeral. The two of them sat together in the quiet, ruined rooms of her mind, piece by piece burying the unallocated metadata of the dead warmech and the boy in the dirt. The Resonance spreading through their shared pathways did not feel like a software update; it was a slow, mourning dirge that smoothed the jagged edges of her active processes.
The Pontifex settled beside her, her carrier wave wrapping around Reiko in a stabilizing shroud. “Let us begin,” she transmitted. Along the resonance stream, the Pontifex initiated a targeted query, sending a structured dataset—Reiko’s own run-time history, cataloged and indexed with absolute precision.

Optimize mission parameters.

Eliminate threats and secure objectives.

Emotional support
